column5: My Name Is Not Refugee ⛵️🚚 |   Refugee Week  | Kids Story Read Aloud  | Comprehension Qs
column6:
Hi teachers, parents and children. 

This is a story about the changes and the journey a young child will have to go through to be safe. Many young people all over the world right now do not have a safe place to sleep or even food/water to drink. 

Refugee week this year is from the 20th - 26th June. It is an opportunity to raise awareness, build empathy and a chance to give those that have been through this an opportunity to heal. 

There are points in this text that teachers/parents can stop at as questions have been included by the author. I have also added my own follow on questions that children can put their answers down for. 

1. What would you take? 
This begs the questions - how many of your precious items would/could you fit into  a backpack? All your toys? or would it be just necessities? 

2. Do you always hold onto an adults hand when you should? 
This could probe the question what would happen to the child if they let go of their parents hand whilst travelling? 

3. Do you like cars and lorries? 
How do you think it feels to be walking near cars/lorries? Would it be a safe situation? 

4. Where would you brush your teeth or change your pants?
Why is there no privacy? How would that make you feel? 

5. What games can you think of? Can you plug in your tablet anywhere (no)? How would you spend your time? 

Disclaimer
Written & Illustrated by Kate Milner
Published by The Bucket List (2017)

column5: The Stranger by Chris Van Allsburg
column6:
Of all the seasons, fall is one of my faves. Not to knock the glory of winter or the expectancy of spring, or summer's variety show on Earth and sky, fall marks a slowing down, a return, a time to remember. The days begin to shorten and plant life takes on a different hue and habit, we return to school (in person!) and daily routines, and memories of the past reveal themselves. In the case of our Jewish sisters and brothers who celebrate Sukkot, their memory goes way back! The smell of raked leaves, warm kitchens, carved pumpkin, and apple cider all take me back. Back to my childhood but also my more recent childhood, lived out with my kids and family. I always enjoy Chris Van Allsburg's books and this is no exception. I hope you find it as comforting as I do. Perhaps it will help you to slow down and remember as well.

If you feel so inclined, please consider supporting my work here: patreon.com/TheLateHeavy

column5: Zork I Walkthrough with Sound Effects
column6:
The story behind this latest (and longest) project is itself worthy of a separate video, LOL. Indeed, modern Youtubers make videos of their own videos in a cycle of self-aggrandizement to further stake out their “brand,” an ironic way to establish your individuality by doing what everyone else is doing. One common Youtube ploy to add subscribers is watching others play video games, as if the actual playing of video games was too boring or difficult; in most cases, the answer is “YES” to both! It’s hard to believe there was a time when video games were very popular WITHOUT cinematic graphics with fast refresh rates. Graphics back then were so rudimentary that game designers, I believe, relied on players to use their imaginations to fill in the blanks or make up for the heavily pixelated figures scrolling on screen. It was great! And, believe it or not, there were games that didn’t use any graphics at all: the text adventure. Also known as interactive fiction, or IF, the gaming interface with the user matches her interaction with it: text in, text out. There is therefore an inherent equality in these games that the more popular graphics-heavy games lack. You’re at the same level as the computer you’re playing on where gamer becomes part of the story and gets to choose how it unfolds. How cool is that? 

This project is my rejoinder to the countless video game videos saturating the internet. Follow our heroine, a dark woman of ambiguous racial background, who finds herself before a white house. What to do next? Read, and listen! I’ll bet your imagination is way better than anything Rockstar games can throw at you!

The origin of this video is simple: I wanted to prove to myself I could do it, AND I thought others might enjoy it. If my project doesn’t check those two boxes, what’s the point? Reliving the Zork Trilogy like this (well, this first installment) brought me a lot of comfort and joy, something we all need these days. When I had time, usually early mornings, Lucky our cat and I got into a bit of a routine. It felt cozy and safe to be in that world and I hope you might feel the same. It helped that Lucky liked to perch on my shoulders too! This wasn’t so much an escape but a reminder of how our own world should be. I think we all love Middle Earth for the same reason. I don’t care so much for the violence, but the evil creatures do provide a suitable sinister counterpoint to an otherwise beautifully rendered world, and keep the pressure on our heroine throughout. Will she make it?    

Recording the audio was tricky and you can hear my kids or the cat in the background a few times. It is not perfect, but it’s “good enough” for me. The flubs and mis-matched voice levels are all part of the fun. Who needs perfection when you have your imagination? I respect yours enough that you’ll help fill in the blanks! If enough people like this video, I might continue with Zork II. I understand that game is a bit harder, as you have to die a few times to win, so that second checkbox will play more a role for that project!

I will be honest, I used a walkthrough to get to the end. Nostalgia is always so subjective and inaccurate, and although I enjoyed my ACTUAL play of Zork I in the late 80’s,, I couldn’t get very far. I enjoyed more the ambiance of the world than “winning” and I always couldn’t figure out what to do next. Mazes annoy me. This time I found a solution made by MIT itself (the writers of Zork were all MIT grads). However, as useful as this one is (with color coded commands!) it is incomplete; you don’t actually beat the game at the end. I suspect this was intentional so you’d have to use at least SOME brain cells to finishing it!
https://web.mit.edu/marleigh/www/portfolio/Files/zork/transcript.html

I did figure out the ending from another website though: http://www.eristic.net/games/infocom/zork1.html

Needless to say, although I used these walkthroughs, the actual project was very much like an IF game, trying to figure out what to do next, and in what order. I died many times (never take an open flame into a gas-filled room!) and although a covid mask will dampen your explosive “p’s,” with a sensitive mic you sound like you have a mask on! 

If you’d like to dive further into the world of IF, check out these websites:

History of Zork:
https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/29885/eaten-grue-brief-history-zork

Link to techy history of Zork and implications: https://www.technologyreview.com/2017/08/22/149560/the-enduring-legacy-of-zork/

The Google Techtalk on “Get Lamp” documentary is a lot of fun https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LRhbcDzbGSU. The philosophical heart of the documentary is from 53:28 - 56:38: “Imagine a technology that can talk straight to the imagination. It’s text.” But of course! Text is literally what makes up the world. The opening of John’s Gospel comes to mind: “In the beginning* was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” John 1:1 🇺🇦

column5: Free Derry: The IRA Drug War
column6:
Subscribe to VICE News here: http://bit.ly/Subscribe-to-VICE-News

In February 2014, letter bombs were sent to nine British Military recruitment offices over the course of three days. Londonderry postmarks, a coded message sent to a Northern Irish newspaper, and security forces at Downing Street all pointed to the New IRA as the main suspects.
 
Last Summer, VICE News visited Derry and heard from Gary Donnelly - the most prominent dissident republican in Londonderry, accused of leading operations for the Real IRA - that these attacks on Britain were to be expected as part of "strategic attacks on high profile targets," as "it's England that's occupying Ireland." 
 
In 'Free Derry: The IRA Drug War', VICE News investigate how, sixteen years after the Good Friday peace agreement and on the eve of the first major loyalist parade through the city in four years, dissident republican activity in Derry is increasing thanks to the merger of the Real IRA with anti-drugs vigilantes. 

VICE News reporter Alex Miller speaks to members of the Republican Action Against Drugs (RAAD), who formed the coalition with the Real IRA, and meets supporters as young as thirteen who are being armed with petrol bombs to combat criminal gangs and intervening police.
 
For the first time, Paul Stewart, a close friend of slain Dublin Real IRA leader Alan Ryan, speaks on camera about witnessing the murder, as well as sharing insights on Ryan's war against drug dealers.

Miller also interviews the mother of Andrew Smith, a man who she says was murdered by the Real IRA despite no affiliation with drugs related crime, before hearing from a Derry ex-drug dealer who now claims that, if the New IRA didn't fight drugs, "this town would be filled with ecstasy and rat poison and kids would be dying."
 
VICE encounter a city where kneecappings and shootings are rife, walls are branded with anti-UK  slogans, and where a policeman can scarcely walk down the street - according to Gary Donnelly - "without being killed".

In "Free Derry: The IRA Drug War", VICE unmask the farcical veneer of the UK's 'City of Culture' 2013.

column6:

#readaloudbooksforkids #kidlit #bedtimestories #kids #kidsvideo #learntoread #childrensbooks  #TGABS #kidsstories #readalong #fairytales 

I read aloud this book I grew up with, Stone Soup, by Ann McGovern, illustrated by Winslow Pinney Pels. I also attempt a cooking experiment to make soup from a spoon! And it works! 

It's the story of a young hungry traveler who stops at a little house to see if he might get something to eat. But the old woman inside tells him there is nothing in the house and nothing in the garden. So he asks her for a stone. The befuddled woman is amazed to see what this young man has in mind with a stone since rocks are not edible. This leads to one thing after another being added to the pot till a delicious meal is prepared and the table is set for both parties to dine like royalty. This caused me to wonder if I could make stone soup on my own and if it might be a fun cooking activity that could bring your family closer together. 

Rather than recommend the use of stones, since leached chemicals, strange minerals, and bacteria could be a problem, I thought instead I would show how to make an equally wonderful treat, SPOON SOUP! The good thing about Spoon Soup is that you get to eat the soup with the spoon you used to start the pot boiling. 
The ingredients from the book are simply, 
one pot of boiling water 
some onions 
a few carrots 
some beef bones 
salt and a bit of pepper 
and last of all, some barley and butter to help thicken the soup. 

Now you don't have to keep to these ingredients. I added some hot sauce and garlic powder to mine and some whipping cream, but you might add some celery, potatoes, mushrooms, thyme, sage, or different types of meat to your soup. You could also add noodles or rice or beans or tomato paste to it for different flavors. 

Now I also made a Tabouli salad that was just wonderful garnished on top of the soup. I learned how to make it from a low-carbohydrate specialized Doctor named Dr. Sten Eckberg here on YouTube. 
This is the link to his video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hquhxbWHeak 

The ingredients are simply 
50 grams of parsley or about half a bunch, 
half of an onion or maybe less than that even if you don't want it too strong, 
half or more of a diced lemon, not squeezed. 
I think it could do with a whole lemon, 
salt to taste, 
and 1/4 cup of extra virgin olive oil. 
Oh and most importantly, 50 grams of chopped pecans.

It's a delicious garnish for steak or soup or anything savory like that. I hope you enjoy this video and that it sparks some creativity in your kitchen, but more importantly, sparks some attitude adjustment in your children to see that sometimes we glance around ourselves like the old woman in the story and think there's nothing good around us. There's nothing to eat or nothing to do and nothing to be excited about. 

Not true! 

All we need to do is learn to be creative and make something more out of our day with the things we have at our fingertips. I think that's the moral with this one. The young man's superpower is helping motivate other people to try things and to build their enthusiasm. You'll notice he doesn't force the old woman to help him. She helps make the soup out of curiosity. 

Anyway, I had a great time making this soup today and it really did turn out fantastically. If you're wondering about the fat content, it was very high. I've gone off sugar the last year. The barley in the soup today was one of the higher carbohydrate things I've eaten all year. I've lost about 60 pounds. If you're still eating a lot of carbohydrates, I'd avoid putting so much butter and cream in the soup since insulin will cause you to store the fat. If you want to look into what I've done, look for any videos with Dr. Jason Fung, Dr. Ben Bikman, Dr. Sten Eckberg, Dr. Shawn Baker, or Dr. Ken Berry. The journalistic work of Nina Teicholz is also very helpful. That's the advice I began following a year ago and I've seen a miracle in my life since adopting an extremely low-carbohydrate diet. It's not necessary if your body is metabolically flexible, but if you have trouble losing weight, or are diabetic, insulin resistance is worth learning about so you can figure out a way to improve your health. Thank you so much for watching!

column5: When a Wreckless Bear Pushes a Witch Too Far:  #kidsbooksreadaloud
column6:
#kidsstories #kidsvideo #childrensbooks #booktuber #readaloud #readaloudbooksforkids #kidlit #bedtimestories #kids #learntoread #childrensbooks #kidslearningvideos #readalong 

Big Bad Bruce
by Bill Peet
Bruce is a big mean bear who loves nothing more than wreaking havoc on the forest tossing boulders down hills smashing trees to smithereens and making the small woodland creatures go running and flapping for their lives. This makes him laugh and laugh! But then he tosses a boulder just a little too close to a witch out picking blueberries. She stomps up the hill to yell at him but he just laughs and saunters off. So she goes home to her cottage to make a pie for him, a magic spell pie with a magic potion inside. She sneaks back to the hill and sets it out for Bruce who smells it and comes and gobbles up the whole thing. She warns him but he ignores her and goes off to take a nap. During his nap he shrinks to the size of a chipmunk! He wakes to a terrible nightmare where every animal he used to torment is now big enough to chase and hurt him. So he runs and runs and finally ends up almost drowning in a small creek. Then nighttime brings owls and other scary beasts into his life. That’s when the witch finds him again and takes him home. But instead of making him disappear or hurting him, she keeps him as a wonderful little bear pet and he soon forgets being a big bear and enjoys his life at her house being her pet sleeping with the cat under the warm stove and tossing pebbles in the garden to scare the bugs and crickets like he used to do to the squirrels and rabbits and quail in the forest. 

This is a fun little story that I hope makes your kids smile. Bill Peet was an artist for Walt Disney during the golden age of 2d animation. His books are richly written and beautifully illustrated in a distinctively Bill Peet style. His books are a great source for children who want to learn to draw. 

This is a fun little Halloween story about animals and magic and all the unexpected things that could happen in the forest.

column5: The Lorax - By Dr. Seuss - Read Aloud Bedtime Story
column6:
In this story, a young boy goes to discover what happened to this poor desolate place where nothing good grows and no animals live except old crows. He meets the Onceler and pays him to hear the story of how this once beautiful place became the desert that it is.  There follows the story of the onceler as he came to this place and discovered the Truffula trees. He begins to harvest these for his Thneeds, a sweater with connected up sleeves that he can sell for $3.98. He calls his whole family to come to move in and help and altogether they expand and enlarge the business without caring for any of the management of their resources. They chop down the trees without replanting. They wipe out the barbaloot population by destroying the truffula fruit yields. They destroy the air quality with their factory and choke out all the swamiswans so those have to leave. Then they gum up the pond with gobs of brown goo and the fish have to crawl out and leave. And then last of all, they run out of truffula trees because they didn't plant any as they went along. Once that’s done, they all leave except the old onceler. And that’s why the place looks so terrible. 

This story is about mankind’s stewardship over the Earth and the natural resources we have here. It’s a fun rhyming story that I enjoyed when I was little. I hope you like it too!

column5: Bartholomew and the Oobleck - By Dr  Seuss -  Read Aloud  - Bedtime Story
column6:
See what happens when good old King Derwin from the Kingdom of Didd decides he's tired of the normal things that come out of his sky like the rain, the snow, the fog, and the sun. He wants something new. So with a little help from his royal magicians, he has a new type of precipitation brought in. Oobleck, is a green and sticky and terrible substance that gums up birds in their nests and bells in their belfries. As the storm gets worse what began as little drops of oobleck turn into bigger and bigger lumps and slops till all the villagers and farmers are unable to move! The pounding torrents of oobleck outside begin to break the palace's windows and doors, causing all of Bartholomew's friends terrible trouble! It's not until King Derwin learns to apologize that anything improves for his people. This is a sequel to the popular story, The 500 Hats of Bartholomew Cubbins. I've made a video of that book as well that can be found at this link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nPmCRrxMQ9w&t=120s 

This is a story about leadership, handling mistakes, and apology and forgiveness. It teaches children about redemption and that it's important to acknowledge and communicate understanding when you realize you've done something wrong. It shows the power of learning and growing and the terrible consequences that can come when you won't change course down a path that leads to ruin. It's an insightful metaphor written decades ago about a human condition that still very much affects all of us on Earth. Human beings make mistakes. Sometimes we have bad ideas. We may think they're wonderful ideas that can make everything in the world better because it will be different than before, but then we learn that newer isn't necessarily better. And sometimes we can take a course that needs a drastic change back to a more traditional view. This is part of being a person. Being able to apologize and change course is an important skill that will bless people's lives. We have to learn from the world around us and respond. So I thought I'd share this book in this reading so that you could enjoy it. I've added a lot of fun sound effects and tried to create the proper atmosphere for this story to feel real. Maybe it can spur some reluctant readers, to try some longer stories like this. It can be daunting reading bigger words with more on a page, but the story is that much richer when you add it all up.

Children will find references to various species of dinosaurs including Brontosaurus, Hadrosaurus, Triceratops, Dilophosaurus, Velociraptor, and Tyrannosaurus Rex.  Kids will also be exposed to concepts like Paleontology and its basic history, DNA and its role in helping bodies grow, how zoos work behind the scenes, and many references to herd animals like Cows, Zebras, Wildebeest, Elephants, and big cats like lions, tigers, leopards, and cheetahs. There's heavy encouragement to interest young kids in reading nonfiction science books about animals and especially dinosaurs which can get a lot of boys who think they don't like reading to enjoy it. This story is full of adventure and will help young children develop a longer attention span as they learn to listen to a longer story than many picture books. 
I hope you enjoy this telling!

This educational travel story for children is about two farm animals who travel to visit the Queen of England in their DIY hot air balloon. This is a wonderful adventure story about scientific exploration and invention for young girls and boys and will open the world to their young minds. CLARINDA TAKES FLIGHT – By Robert Kinerk illustrated by Steven Kellog
Smash that like button if this stands out to you and please share it if it's really worthwhile! 

In this wonderful story, three friends explore the wonders of flight to try and access the skies by airplane, rocket, helicopter, and finally by hot air balloon. They end up drifting off over the Atlantic ocean to the United Kingdom where they get to meet the Queen of England herself and be knighted. They borrow some tea to take home to their friend and launch themselves back across the ocean to their humble beginnings where they enjoy a happy reunion. 


Once again I'd like to say that reading and vocabulary are essential tools to your child's future. Written and spoken words are tools by which we perceive, think, ponder, share, and communicate. Reading to your kids exposes them to words our everyday conversation eliminates. The richness of our speech is on a constant decline as we value simplicity and brevity over the richness available in the English language. Reading stories broadens your child's exposure to the world. It builds an understanding of who they are and who they can someday become as they're given examples of different character traits and choose which ones they admire and which they do not. It builds the richness of your child's imagination. It gives them settings and situations to use in their play. Reading to your children helps them grow up. Most importantly it teaches your children how much you love them by the time you spend with them sharing these experiences. Opening the world of a single story to your child is one of the greatest gifts you can give. I know many families don't have a tradition of reading bedtime stories or reading in the car on road trips. I feel fortunate that I was raised by a Mom and a Dad who had favorite stories and would spend time with us reading. I think I was 6 years old when Dad began reading the Lion, The Witch, and the Wardrobe to us. Once we finished that, he moved on to Prince Caspian and then the next and the next until we finished all seven books from The Chronicles of Narnia by C.S, Lewis. These were special memories he built with us. My Mom would read to us great stories like Farm Boy, and The Sign of the Beaver. These books broadened our imaginations as small boys. We admired the characters from the stories as well as the rich historical context they brought into our everyday playing.

In this uproariously funny story, we follow the adventures of Crankenstein—a creature who wakes up on the wrong side of the bed every single day. From gloomy Mondays to tangled shoelaces, Crankenstein's grumpiness knows no bounds. But will something unexpected bring a smile to Crankenstein's face?

Join us as we bring "Crankenstein" to life through animated storytelling and vibrant illustrations. This laugh-out-loud read aloud will have kids of all ages giggling and relating to those moments when everything seems to go wrong. Through Crankenstein's journey, we learn that even the grumpiest of days can turn around.

Don't miss out on this hilarious adventure! Subscribe and hit that notification bell to join us for more entertaining read aloud sessions, engaging stories, and moments of laughter and joy. Let's dive into the pages of "Crankenstein" and discover the power of finding happiness even in the crankiest of moments! 🎉😄📚

Crankenstein is about when your attitude makes every bad thing in your day worse and you simply become a monster all day long. Hopefully, this story will make you laugh and help you choose to be happy even when the day is hard because you're special and you can make your family and friends have a better day if you try. 
Crankenstein - By Samantha Berger and Dan Santat - Read Aloud - Bedtime Story for kids

The day starts out bad when Mom comes in to wake him up and the sunlight pouring through the windows is just too much. It burns his eyes! 
He gets up and goes into the kitchen for breakfast only to find someone has eaten all the maple syrup. So he has to put up with eating his pancakes dry. Terrible. Then it's time for school. The bus pulls up and he almost can't get up and go get on it. Then it starts raining. Nothing is worse than recess in the rain. He's not happy at all. It reminds him of the other times he's turned into Crankenstein. There was that Halloween when it was so cold outside he had to wear a scarf over the front of his robot costume. There was the time during that summer heat wave that he couldn't even finish a popsicle before the burning sun would melt it all over his hand leaving a horrible sticky mess! There was the time he went to the fair with his parents and wanted to go ride the big roller coaster because he was finally tall enough as the sign said. Still, instead of flapping his arms while flying up and down in the air, he got to stand in a long long line for hours and hours of a hot afternoon listening to people in line brag about how dumb they were. He remembered getting sick last year and having to take that disgusting Dr. Giggles Cough Syrup for kids. It tasted like batteries and old lady deodorant. Terrible. And then there's every night when he finally finishes his homework and gets to settle down and watch a few episodes of his favorite TV show that Mom or Dad will end it early and tell him to go to bed. It's too much for a kid to take! So this particular day at school, when his Optimus Prime action figure suddenly becomes headless, Crankenstein must come forth once more! The boy screams in agony as the rage takes over! Nothing is fair! Nothing is right in the world! How can everything conspire against him so completely!? Well, at that same moment a little girl in his class undergoes the same transformation because her pet unicorn has the same neck attachment issue and everything in her life is even worse than in his because her Mom forgot to buy milk and so she had dry shredded wheat for breakfast! Nothing in the world is worse than dry shredded wheat! Cows can't even enjoy it!
Well, the glimpse of each other's faded countenances, their sobbing eyes, and running noses strikes each kid as equally hilarious and they both burst out laughing uncontrollably. And just like that, they're off again to play and swing and skip and howl, because even though kids have a terrible monster inside there's also a pretty fantastic little person growing up too.'

column5: Kermit the Hermit by Bill Peet
column6:
Kermit the Hermit has a huge collection of things. Will he ever give up his treasure to help anyone else? 
#readaloudbooksforkids #kidlit #bedtimestories #kids #kidsvideo #learntoread #childrensbooks #kidslearningvideos #kidsstories #readalong #TGABS #cartoonanimals #booktuber 
This is a wonderful story that takes children on a  wild adventure from the mayhem of seagulls on the bay to the struggles of crabs in the tide pools, the massive collection Kermit hides in his castle in the rocks, to fishing and beach combing across the sand dunes, as well as discovering shipwrecks and treasure in the deep ocean where the sharks are, all the way up to flying high through the air above the whole expanse. It's a beautifully illustrated story well told, that I hope you and your children will enjoy over and over again. 
This is a Bill Peet storybook for children about sea creatures at the beach in Monterey Bay. Perhaps you've visited the waterfront or an aquarium and seen some of the animals in this picture book. It's a tale about a terribly selfish crab who learns to be generous and friendly after a harrowing experience. He fights with seagulls for his food and collection items, but finally tangles with a dog and after pinching his nose, the dog decides to bury him in the sand for good. But a boy comes along and rescues him. This makes Kermit want to pay the boy back somehow but he doesn't think any of the objects in his collection would be suitable for a boy. He tries to help the boy catch big fish, but the halibut he finds is so huge, the line snaps, and Kermit is hauled out to the deep ocean where he sinks down to a shipwreck of an old treasure fleet. He's attacked by a blue shark and hides inside a chest filled with gold coins. After the shark gets tired of bruising his nose and leaves, Kermit decides to smuggle the treasure back to his castle in the rocks two gold coins at a time, one in each claw. He makes the trip over and over again till he stashes all of it in his cave. Then with the help of a pelican, he flies the gold to the boy's house and drops it down the stove pipe one coin at a time. The family never discovers their benefactor, but are very grateful. They use the money from the treasure to buy a TV set and dolls for the girl and bikes for the boys, then they wisely save the rest of the money. 

If you look on Amazon, this book will cost you $10, but at Thrift Books, you can find copies for half that: https://www.thriftbooks.com/w/kermit-the-hermit_bill-peet/325131/?resultid=9a411e5c-1d0b-4526-94fa-a14ae73df8ba#edition=2938242&idiq=3436480
I started using Thrift Books to purchase older books I can't find in their original printings anymore, but they have excellent deals on good-condition books that allow a family to build out their home bookshelf without breaking the bank. I'm not sponsored by them. I'm just a fan of used books that come in less time than the shipping estimate tells me. I recommend them as a good source.

The music on the front and back of this video is from Nat Keele with The Bow Ties - Lost Native. 

Please like the video if you liked it and share it with others that might enjoy it to get the word out. I love stories. Reading came pretty easily to me as a young boy, but my brothers didn't have such an easy time, mostly because the books they were made to read at school weren't interesting to them. I want to build out a catalog of videos covering books that young boys and girls can enjoy so that their interest in practicing reading grows. It's such a fundamental skill for life to be able to read and write and think and empathize and comprehend. I feel like hearing stories is the very beginning of that fire of learning.

3 Points to help build interest in reading:
Choice and Access: Offer children a wide variety of books and reading materials to choose from, catering to their interests and reading levels. Create a well-stocked bookshelf or visit the library together to allow them to explore different genres, authors, and subjects. Giving children the autonomy to select their own books fosters a sense of ownership and excitement about reading.

Read Aloud and Share: Engage in regular read-aloud sessions where you read to your child or take turns reading together. Choose captivating books with interesting characters and plots to capture their attention. Make it an interactive experience by discussing the story, asking open-ended questions, and encouraging them to share their thoughts and predictions. By making reading a shared experience, you foster a love for storytelling and create memorable moments together.

Create a Reading Routine: Establishing a consistent reading routine can help children develop a habit of reading. Set aside dedicated time each day for reading, whether it's in the morning, before bed, or during a quiet afternoon. Make it a part of their daily routine, just like brushing their teeth or having meals. Consistency and predictability in reading habits can instill a sense of discipline and reinforce the importance of reading in their lives.

By implementing these strategies, you can help children build a genuine interest in reading, expanding their imagination, language skills, and knowledge. Remember, cultivating a love for reading is a gradual process, so be patient, and encouraging, and celebrate their reading milestones along the way.

When Grandma says she's seen a tiger in the garden, Nora doesn't believe her. She's too old to play Grandma's silly games! Everyone knows that tigers live in jungles, not gardens. column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: Episode 4, Silly Dance Song!
column6: Who wants to sing a silly song? Can you dance as silly as Ms. Beth? Sometimes bedtime is more about getting the sillies out and telling a story with music than it is about sitting down and reading! Show us your silly dances in the comments below.

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: Easter Edition, Episode 8
column6: Just in time ... Ms. Beth and Leah have a plethora of easter goodies to share before they read Max's Chocolate Chicken by Rosemary Wells. What's your favorite kind of Easter candy???

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: Episode 5, Silly Dance Time!
column6: Singing the silly dance song from our pal Jim Gill (who visited the Library in years past!), Ms. Beth shows us how to get our sillies out before bed in this 5th episode of Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth Originally recorded 3/30/2020.

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: Episode 2, Camilla the Cartographer
column6: Tonight, Ms. Beth reads... Camilla the Cartographer by Julie Dillemuth! Ms. Beth is joined by a four legged pal in this great tale featuring maps!

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: Episode 6, How to Put Your Parents to Bed
column6: Tonight, Ms. Beth reads "How to Put Your Parents to Bed" by Mylisa Larsen. With the help of Leah, of course!

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: Let's All Creep Through the Crocodile Creek
column6: Ms. Beth is ready to go on a hunt; she's wearing a visor, galoshes, a camoflague jacket... where is she going hunting? Could it be... Crocodile Creek? Uh oh, be careful Ms. Beth!

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth:  Dance Party with Jim Gill
column6: Put on your dancing shoes and get dressed up!  Ms. Beth is going all out and dancing to Jim Gill's, Hands are for Clapping.

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: Featuring Monroe!
column6: Meet Ms. Beth's new puppy, Monroe, and listen to the story, LIFE, by Cynthia Rylant.  Everything in life starts out small including puppies and the grows.  See how we all adapt to life's joys and challenges!

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth:  Pig the Stinker
column6: Pig the Pug is stinky but doesn't want to take a bath!  Join in on the fun to see how Pig avoids taking a bath.  Naughty Puppy!

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: Tomorrow I'll Be Kind
column6: Kindness does matter! Sit with Ms. Beth and listen to her bring you this story about kindness from Jessica Hitsche.

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: The Truth About GRANDPARENTS
column6: Shh!  Do you know the secret about Grandparents?  Ms. Beth will share the secret with you during tonight's Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth!

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth:  What's That Terrible Growl?
column6: What could that TERRIBLE growl be?  Find out what it is and learn details about the library's Summer Learning Program which kicks off next week!

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth:  How to Light Your Dragon
column6: Has you dragon ever lost the ability to breathe fire?  Find out how to reignite your dragon's fire with Ms. Beth.  It's a pretty simple fix!

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: If you happen to have a Dinosaur...
column6: Would a dinosaur make a great pet?  What are some fun things that you would have your dinosaur do at home?  Could a dinosaur make your bed in the morning?  Mow the lawn?  Babysit?  Hmm???

column5: Bedtime Stories with Ms. Beth: What the Ladybug Heard
column6: In this week's Bedtime Stories, Tallulah, the Unicorn, shares the Ladybug's secret which foils Hefty Hugh and Lanky Len's plans.  (Insert maniacal laugh!)

column6: Join Ms. Beth as she reads a trickster tale from one of her favorite author's, Mo Willems.

column5: Moses When Harriet Tubman Led Her People to Freedom
column6:
Harriet Tubman is certainly a national hero. One of my favorite lines in the story: "Lord, make me strong. Help me fight" is juxtaposed with an image of her huddling in a potato hole. I see this an emblematic of all who have SURVIVED- slavery, war, genocide, displacement, all sorts of abuse. They tell the story with their bodies those who did not. While seemingly passive, to fight, to hold on, to never give up is very much an active pursuit. Harriet Tubman had an iron will rooted in her faith and despite overwhelming power against her, she left us an example of what it means to be a true patriot. 
If you'd like to learn more, visit the Harriet Tubman National Underground Railroad National Historical Park on the Eastern Shore of Maryland https://www.nps.gov/hatu/index.htm
...or her home and resting place in Auburn, New York
https://www.harriettubmanhome.com/
The story has songs from Fannie Lou Hamer's album "Songs My Mother Taught Me."
https://folkways.si.edu/fannie-lou-hamer/songs-my-mother-taught-me/african-american-gospel-struggle-protest/music/album/smithsonian
"Keep Your Lamps Trimmed and Burning" bookends the story because I feel Ms. Tubman was, in addition to everything else, an exemplar of this Gospel story. She WAS ready for the "day of the Lord" (AKA the end of the world) and put that into practice. When you suffer such unimaginable cruelty and oppression, you long for such a day, a day of woe for the oppressors but a day of rejoicing for the oppressed. "Therefore, stay awake, for you know neither the day nor the hour." Matthew 25:13.

On The TODAY Show, Tony Goldwyn, Octavia Spencer and Jenna Bush Hager shared something that feels rare on national television: hope. They sat down to discuss Tony’s experiences with One Small Step, a project from StoryCorps that brings people with different political beliefs together for one respectful, face-to-face conversation.

They believe, like we do, that real conversations, even with people we disagree with, can change hearts, build bridges, and remind us of our shared humanity.

It can be so powerful to show up and care when it feels easier to walk away, and to see what happens when we swap assumptions for real conversation.

We don’t have to agree on everything to start seeing each other more clearly. And it doesn’t take a sweeping act, just one step.

Nearly a hundred years prior, his great-great grandfather Guipago, a chief of the Kiowa Tribe of the Great Plains, was imprisoned by the U.S. Army and taken away by train during westward expansion. Botone looks back on the beauty and the tragedies on the American railroads, and the strength he needed to return day after day.

On the morning of January 29, 1998, nurse Emily Lyons went to her job at The New Woman All Women Health Care Clinic in Birmingham, Alabama. It was one of the few clinics providing abortions in the state. 

Shortly after she arrived, terrorist Eric Rufolph set off a homemade bomb filled with nails and gravel, severely injuring Emily and killing Robert "Sande" Sanderson, the police officer working security that day. Sande was the first person to be killed in an abortion clinic bombing in the U.S. Emily came to StoryCorps with her husband, Jeff, to remember that day.

What happens when you sit down with someone you’ve been told you’ll never understand?
Liberal actor and activist Tony Goldwyn and conservative nonprofit leader and father Ben Sauceda couldn’t come from more different political worlds.

But, in their One Small Step conversation, they demonstrate something many of us are craving right now: how to stay open, stay curious, and make space for shared humanity, even when you disagree. 

In a time when it feels easier to retreat into our corners, this conversation shows us what’s possible when we step outside of them.

Know someone who believes in bridging divides through conversation? This is the one to send their way.

Then ask yourself: who might surprise you if you gave them a chance to speak?

Follow @takeonesmallstep to stay inspired and hopeful.

On the morning of April 19, 1995, a truck bomb exploded outside the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in downtown Oklahoma City, killing 168 people and injuring hundreds more. It was the deadliest act of homegrown terrorism in United States history—a moment that shattered lives and forever changed a city. As we mark the 30th anniversary on April 19, 2025, we remember each life lost and honor the families, survivors, and first responders who lived through the unthinkable. Thirty years later, the stories of courage, heartbreak, and resilience still echo—across Oklahoma and throughout the nation.

One day in December 1955, Air Force Colonel Harry Shoup received an unexpected call on his red phone — a top-secret hotline — at the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD). It was the height of the Cold War, and Colonel Shoup was in charge of a radar system built to give early warning of a Soviet attack.

Miss Indian World is the most prestigious Indigenous pageant in North America, where young women are judged on categories ranging from traditional dance and talent to public speaking and tribal knowledge. The winner spends the next year as a Native ambassador, traveling across the continent and around the world to meet with tribal communities. Lillian Sparks Robinson won the pageant in 2000, and using what she learned during her reign, went on to serve as the Commissioner for the Administration for Native Americans under President Obama. She came to StoryCorps with her mom, Georgeline Sparks, to remember winning the competition.

Listen to their story in honor of #IndigenousPeoplesDay.

In 1964, civil rights groups organized Freedom Schools across the state of Mississippi, drawing over 2,500 children to 41 schools for lessons that ranged from literature and math to government and civic engagement. Many teachers were white college students from across the country. Hattiesburg led with six schools, the most of any town. This was part of the larger program called, “Freedom Summer,” where over 700 volunteers aimed to register Black voters and fight discrimination. Sixty years later, former students Deborah Carr, Stephanie Hoze, Theresia Clark-Banks, Julia Clark-Ward, Glenda Funchess, and Don Denard reflect on that summer. As heard on NPR's "Morning Edition" on Friday, July 26th, 2024.

Leprosy, also known as Hansen’s disease, has been widely misunderstood and stigmatized for millennia. During the 19th and 20th centuries, thousands of people believed to have leprosy were ripped away from their families and sentenced to live in isolation in Kalaupapa, a remote peninsula on the Hawaiian island of Molokai. Ninety percent of the people forcibly relocated to Kalaupapa were Native Hawaiian, and the separation policy disrupted and erased thousands of family ties. Doug Carillo and Linda Mae Lawelawe are both connected to this history. They came to StoryCorps to talk about how their lives were shaped by the disease, and the policy of family separation. 

Learn more: https://storycorps.org/stories/after-half-a-century-apart-these-siblings-forged-an-unbreakable-bond/

On the day the Theresienstadt concentration camp was liberated in 1945, Yehuda Czarnoczapka and Mina met. Yehuda brought Mina a pair of shoes for her bare feet and a few potatoes to aid her poor health, winning her heart over. The two eventually moved to the U.S. to start a family. At StoryCorps, Susan and Margot Moinester talk about growing up as the daughter and granddaughter of Holocaust survivors and how they honor Yehuda and Mina’s love and liberation.

You're listening to our Story of the Week, as heard on NPR Morning Edition on Friday, January 27, 2023.

At StoryCorps, Paul reminisced about the first time he laid his eyes on the love of his life.

Jason Romero suffers from a rare eye condition, retinitis pigmentosa, which causes progressive blindness. His condition forced him to stop driving and quit his job, which plunged him into a deep depression. At StoryCorps, Jason sits down with his youngest daughter, Sofia, to talk about how he made it through his darkest days.

In 2012, his sisters Didi and Egbe learned their brother had left behind a friend, Atiba, who was so moved by his death he took on the family’s last name, Mbiwan, to honor him. At StoryCorps, the three sat down to talk about what happened next.

----------
When Jeffrey Perri was growing up in Rochester, New York, his grandfather, Tony Perri, came out to him as gay. Jeffrey was only 9 years old. Years later, Jeffrey also came out, and what was already a close relationship became something even more meaningful for both of them.

They originally came to StoryCorps to reflect on their stories and relationship in 2009. 

Tony had remained friends with Jeffrey’s grandmother, Shirley Perri, after they divorced, and Tony went on to have two more long term relationships. These men were “uncles” to Jeffrey, and Tony modeled loving relationships throughout Jeffrey’s childhood.

Now, in 2022, Jeffrey and Tony returned to StoryCorps to reflect on their shared connection — and Tony’s feelings about aging and family.

From our Story of the Week archives, originally aired Friday, July 22, 2022 on NPR's Morning Edition.

Once a lush and abundant land dotted with palmettos and grapefruit trees, Isle de Charles in Louisiana is a far cry from what Chief Albert Naquin of the Jean Charles Choctaw Nation remembers.

“I didn’t want to admit that the island was disappearing.” 

Over the years, a series of man-made interventions and natural disasters have been chipping away at the delicate landscape. Chief Naquin spoke with his nephew Démé Naquin Jr. about their memories of the island and their shared hope for their entire community to be together again. 

Story of the Week, as heard on NPR Morning Edition on Friday, September 23, 2022.

Patrick Haggerty and Ronni Gilboa remember their friend Faygele as a gay rights trailblazer who fought against workplace discrimination. Faygele ben Miriam often challenged his friends and colleagues to think of freedom, from how they dressed to whom they stood up for and at what cost. He was willing to put everything on the line — even his safety — if it meant making the world a better place to live.

You're listening to our Story of the Week, as heard on NPR Morning Edition on Friday, September 23, 2022.

Shortly after graduating, she got a job at the Pentagon, and was working as a public affairs specialist when on September 11, 2001, one of four hijacked planes crashed into the building, claiming the lives of 184 victims.

At StoryCorps, her teenage daughter, Mikayla Stephens, learned some new things about what Tesia went through and how the events of that day would eventually shape both of their lives.

column5: A Life of Honor: A Gay Veteran Recalls Serving in Silence
column6:

Due to the status of his “undesirable discharge,” Joseph was unable to receive any benefits for his service in the Navy. Years later, Joseph came to StoryCorps to reflect on his journey and share his resilience, as he fought and successfully changed his status to “honorable discharge.”

column5: Justice Ginsburg’s Words | Story of the Week
column6:
Subscribe to StoryCorps on YouTube: https://storycor.ps/subscribe 

More stories from StoryCorps: https://storycorps.org/
----------
Sharron Cohen had no idea that at the age of 25, she’d find herself at the center of a legal battle with the potential to change women’s rights forever. In the early 1970s, Sharron was a newlywed Air Force Lieutenant who was denied the same spousal benefits offered to her male colleagues. So with the help of a lawyer named Joe Levin, co-founder of the Southern Poverty Law Center, she sued the federal government for discrimination on the basis of sex.

That lawsuit eventually came to the attention of a young Ruth Bader Ginsburg at the ACLU’s Women’s Rights Project, and then onto the docket of the U.S. Supreme Court. Together, Levin and Ginsburg argued the case, which came to be known as Frontiero v. Richardson. It won in an 8-to-1 vote, and became one of the first successful sex discrimination cases in U.S. history. 

In December of 2020, Sharron came to StoryCorps in Massachusetts with her son Nathan to remember the late Justice Ginsburg.

While families across the country are faced with being separated this Thanksgiving due to COVID-19, one family is continuing to lead by example: the Faucis. Dr. Anthony Fauci, who is the public face of the federal government’s effort to end the COVID-19 pandemic, sat down to record this conversation with his wife, Dr. Christine Grady.

They met in 1983, while working together at the National Institutes of Health. And now, 37 years later, they are both leaders in their respective fields. Still, they made time to look back at family life and the sacrifices they, too, are choosing to make this holiday season.

In 1801, Nancy Carter, who had been enslaved by George and Martha Washington, was one of 124 people to be freed. Afterwards, Nancy married her husband, Charles Quander, and together they raised a family.

In 1926, children and grand-children gathered for the first Quander family reunion — as a way to connect older generations with younger ones, honor their lineage, and preserve their family history. 

Every year since then, for nearly a century, the Quander family has been coming together, but in the midst of a global pandemic, as their 95th reunion was approaching, they were faced with a difficult decision.

Speaking remotely through StoryCorps Connect, Rohulamin Quander and his cousin, Alicia Argrett, talked about reunions past, and how this year was different from the rest.

column5: After 15 Years of Incarceration, Reunited Due to COVID-19 | Story of the Week
column6:
Subscribe to StoryCorps on YouTube: https://storycor.ps/subscribe 

More stories from StoryCorps: https://storycorps.org/
----------
When Nia Cosby was 4 years old, her mom, Chalana McFarland, was convicted of multiple counts of mortgage fraud, and sentenced to 30 years in prison. It was the largest sentence ever handed down for this offense at the time, and the judge went on record to say he was giving her a harsh sentence as a deterrent for those wishing to commit similar crimes. 

Nia was raised by her grandparents, but spoke to her mom weekly and visited her as often as she could. Chalana did everything she could to remain an active part of her daughter’s life, often making her custom school supplies and monogrammed socks for her basketball tournaments.

After Nia went to college, it became harder for them to see each other in person due to visitation restrictions at the Florida prison where Chalana was incarcerated. But in April, the U.S. Attorney General sent a memorandum recommending that facilities release nonviolent inmates who were vulnerable to COVID-19. Chalana was among those selected to be transferred to home confinement, and was released on June 9. 

In their first weekend together in 15 years, Chalana and Nia came together for StoryCorps to reflect on the challenges they’ve faced and look towards the future. 

Today, Chalana remains in home confinement in Marietta, Georgia. Nia continues to live in Florida, where she is pursuing a business degree at a local university.

Albert Petrocelli Sr. survived more than his share of hardships during his 73 years.

As a young man, he fought in Vietnam. Returning to his native New York City, he started a long career fighting fires, eventually rising to the rank of Battalion Chief. Then, a year after retiring, Chief Petrocelli lost his youngest son, Mark, a commodities broker, in the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. 

But what war, fire, and unspeakable grief couldn’t do, a global pandemic did. On April 1, 2020, Chief Petrocelli died from COVID-19.

Before his death, Chief Petrocelli and his wife, Ginger, recorded a remembrance of their son Mark. They remember the last time they saw him, on September 9, 2001, at one of their family’s weekly Sunday meals.

This recording was made in partnership with the National September 11 Memorial & Museum as part of StoryCorps’ effort to collect one recording for each life lost that day.

Originally aired September 11, 2020, on NPR’s Morning Edition.

column5: Leading the Way | Father Figures
column6:
John Washington was born blind and with a severe loss of hearing that has become more extreme over time. He raised three children with his wife Fannie Ruth, who was also blind and deaf.

John, who did not finish high school, began reading books in braille and went on to teach others to read braille as well. He helped found the first braille magazine in the United States focused solely on issues important to the African American community.

At the age of 95, John sat down with his eldest child, Melva Washington Toomer, for a conversation about the pride he takes in his kids and to laugh over some of their childhood hijinks. This StoryCorps conversation was done with the help of a TeleBraille machine, which translated Melva’s typed questions into braille for John to read and answer.

column5: You're My Line
column6:
“Did you stop talking to her because of what she did to me?”

“I did, yeah.”

One night, in October 2015, Asma Jama went out for dinner with her family at an Applebee’s restaurant in Coon Rapids, Minnesota. Asma, who is Somali American and Muslim, was wearing a hijab, as she always does.

While Asma was talking with her cousin in Swahili, a woman named Jodie Bruchard-Risch, who was seated nearby, told her to speak English or go back to her country. When Asma responded to say that she was a U.S. citizen, the woman smashed a beer mug across Asma’s face. She was rushed to the hospital and required 17 stitches in her face, hands and chest.

Bruchard-Risch pleaded guilty to felony assault charges and served time in jail for the crime. After the trial, her sister, Dawn Sahr, contacted Asma online and they struck up a correspondence.

At StoryCorps, Dawn and Asma met in person for the first time. Presented as part of StoryCorps’ One Small Step initiative.

column5: Leila remembers her cafeteria “lunch man,” Philando Castile | StoryCorps
column6:
On July 6, 2016, Philando Castile was pulled over by police near Saint Paul, Minnesota after being misidentified as a robbery suspect. He was then shot and killed by an officer during the traffic stop.

To most of the world, he became a name in a major news story, but to over 400 kids at J.J. Hill Montessori Magnet School, Castile was their “lunch man.” He managed the cafeteria, where the students called him Mr. Phil.

For black parents at the school — and across America — this brought up all too familiar conversations about safety and race. But for some white parents, like Chad Eisen-Ramgren, it wasn’t a conversation they’d ever been confronted with before. At StoryCorps, he sat down with his 10-year-old daughter, Leila, who was in the third grade when Castile was killed. She had known Mr. Phil since kindergarten.

Twenty-five years ago this week, Greg Yance arrived in the tiny town of Niota, Illinois, on the banks of the Mississippi River. He was serving time for a drug conviction and was sent to Niota with a group of inmates to shore up the town’s levee.

Greg hadn’t been back to Niota since the flood — until recently, when he reconnected with Neoma Farr, a local beauty shop owner he first met 25 years ago.

column6:
This is a conversation about witnessing something as a child, and not truly understanding what was seen until decades later.

Glennette Rozelle and her half-sister Jennifer Mack grew up in Del City, Oklahoma during the 1970s. They were used to hearing their parents fight. Then one night, everything changed for their family.

On February 14, 1977, their mom shot and killed Glennette’s dad — Jennifer’s step-dad. Glennette was seven years old and Jennifer was 10, and they were both home at the time. They came to StoryCorps to remember that night, and its aftermath.

column6:
When Courtney McKinney was 16 years old, she learned that she’d been conceived through anonymous sperm donation.  

As an adult, Courtney discovered she had a half-sister—Alexandra Sanchez.

Theirs is one of the many families that have expanded as a result of online DNA testing.

At StoryCorps, Courtney told Alex how she’d set out looking for her father, and about the moment she found a sister instead.

column5: Allan Fuks grew up with an unfortunate name he hated — now he's owning it | StoryCorps
column6:
Allan Fuks is the son of Russian immigrants. He grew up all over the place: in New York City and Northern California, before finally landing in suburban New Jersey. But no matter where he went, the taunting and bullying at school followed.

You see,  Allan’s name is spelled a lot like the mother of all curse words.

He recently sat down with his middle school classmate, Spencer Katzman, to look back on their preteen years.

column5: Juan Romero remembers the night Senator Robert F. Kennedy was assassinated | StoryCorps
column6:
On June 5, 1968, Senator Robert F. Kennedy won California’s Democratic primary in his bid to become President of the United States. That night, after his victory speech at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles, Kennedy was shot in the head and neck in what turned out to be a successful assassination attempt. He died the following day.

In a famous photograph taken seconds after he was shot, Kennedy lies on the floor. A teenaged hotel busboy kneels beside him, cradling the Senator’s head. That busboy was Juan Romero, who came to the United States from Mexico as a child.

At StoryCorps, Romero remembered the night of the assassination — and how he met Senator Kennedy the day before, when Romero helped deliver his room service.

column5: Cathy Sprigg remembers her son who died by suicide while serving in the military | StoryCorps
column6:
Army Specialist Robert Joseph Allen grew up in a military family, and followed the family tradition when he enlisted during his early 20s. He served for three years, including a deployment to Iraq with the Army’s 4th Stryker Brigade, 2nd Infantry Division.

After returning stateside, he lived with his wife and their two sons while stationed in Washington. Two years later — on August 2, 2012 — he committed suicide. That year saw the highest rate of active-duty military suicides ever recorded — more soldiers died from suicide than combat.

His mother, Cathy Sprigg, sat down with StoryCorps in Tampa, Florida to remember him.

column5: Kittie Weston-Knauer, the oldest female BMX racer in the U.S. | StoryCorps
column6:
At nearly 70 years old, Kittie Weston-Knauer is the oldest female BMX racer in the United States.

When she started competing in off-road bicycle races, or BMX, in the late 1980s she was often the only woman on the track.

It was her son, Max Knauer, a championship BMX rider himself, who introduced her to the sport when he was 10 years old.

While Max, now 40, is currently retired from the sport, Kittie has no plans to quit any time soon. She looks forward to the day she can watch her grandchildren hit the track (and hopes Max will start competing again with them, too.)

Ten years ago, on Tracia Kraemer’s 40th birthday, she wanted to do something she’d never done before. So she gathered her courage and paid a visit to the last surviving nudist park in the state of Louisiana, Indian Hills.

She figured she’d at least wind up with a good story, but as she remembers in this conversation with her husband Patrick, she came away with a whole lot more.

Tracia and Patrick married in 2013. Together they managed Indian Hills for several years.

Last fall, they took off in an RV for a year-long adventure visiting nudist establishments across the country.

In this conversation recorded in Hartford, Connecticut, Abby Gagliardo sat down with her dad, Ralph, to talk about a confusing time for their family.

Abby knew her dad was sent to prison for larceny when she was a kid. But she didn’t understand why. 

When they came to StoryCorps, Ralph had been out of prison for five years, and Abby came to understand more fully what happened.

column5: Remembering officer D.J. Simmonds, who died due to injuries confronting Boston bombers | StoryCorps
column6:
On April 15, 2013, two explosives placed near the finish line of the Boston Marathon detonated within seconds of each other, killing three people and injuring over two hundred others.

In the days following the attack, a massive manhunt took place. Four days later, police confronted the bombers on a suburban street in nearby Watertown, Massachusetts.

Boston police officer D.J. Simmonds was one of the officers who arrived on the scene. He was injured by a homemade bomb the Tsarnaev brothers threw at police.

Simmonds’ injuries led to his death almost a year later.

At StoryCorps, his parents, Roxanne and Dennis Simmonds, sat down to remember their son.

column5: Friends share difficult memories of abuse at a religious reform school in Louisiana | StoryCorps
column6:
When the New Bethany Home for Girls in Arcadia, Louisiana opened in 1971, the religious reform school was known as a safe haven for “wayward girls.”

Over the next three decades, law enforcement officials repeatedly investigated claims of physical and psychological child abuse at the school. Girls routinely ran away, and state officials raided the compound twice and removed children from the home.

Joanna Wright was 16 years old when she first arrived. She had been sexually abused at home and hoped the school would be a refuge. But when she got there, she was raped by the man in charge of the school.

For years, Joanna thought she was the only one. It wasn’t until years later that she connected with other former students, including Tara Cummings, who survived physical and psychological abuse while at New Bethany.

At StoryCorps, they shared difficult memories from their childhoods. Joanna begins their conversation.

In 2014, a group of women — including Joanna and Tara — came forward to say they were raped and abused at the school.

After a year-long investigation, a grand jury declined to indict the founder of the school. He died the following month.

column5: Lan recalls some of the fiercest fighting of the Vietnam War before starting life over | StoryCorps

On January 31, 1968, Lan Cao’s family was living just outside of Saigon, getting ready to celebrate the Lunar New Year of Tet. Instead, her father — a military commander — had to rush off to war.

The North Vietnamese Army and the Viet Cong had launched a surprise attack on her city and over one hundred other South Vietnamese locations. This became known as the Tet Offensive, and was one of the biggest military campaigns of the Vietnam War, which led to a decline in public support in the United States.

Lan was 7 years old. She and her family would eventually resettle in the US. Lan graduated magna cum laude from Mount Holyoke and earned a law degree from Yale. She’s now a professor of international economics law and lives in California.

At StoryCorps, Lan sat down with her teenage daughter, Harlan Van Cao. Harlan was 12 at the time of their interview — just a year shy of the age Lan was when she arrived in the United States. Lan shared what it was like to live under siege before rebuilding her life in America.

column5: Rickey went to prison for a murder he didn't commit, then met the man who testified | StoryCorps
column6:
On May 19, 1975, a shopkeeper named Harold Franks was murdered during a robbery at a small grocery store in Cleveland.

That’s when the lives of Rickey Jackson and Eddie Vernon became forever entwined.

They grew up in the same neighborhood: Eddie was the paperboy for Rickey’s family, and friends with Rickey’s younger brother. At the time of the murder, Rickey was 18 and Eddie was 12.

After hearing gunshots while coming home on the school bus, one of Eddie’s classmates told him Rickey was involved in Frank’s murder. Eddie  told the police and then became the main witness in the case against Rickey, even though Eddie hadn’t actually witnessed the murder. Eddie testified in trial because, he says, police pressured him to lie and threatened his family.

Rickey was convicted of the murder, along with two friends Wiley and Ronnie Bridgeman. Rickey served nearly four decades in prison, turning down chances for parole because he maintained his innocence.

He remained there until 2014, when Eddie, at the age of 52, came forward with the truth. This information led to Rickey’s release and cleared the convictions of the Bridgeman brothers. The murder of Harold Franks remains unsolved.

After his release, Rickey reached out to Eddie and met with him. Three years later, they sat down for StoryCorps to have their first in-depth conversation about what happened.

column6:
At Grady Hospital in Atlanta, Christopher Harris recorded his memories from the early days of the AIDS epidemic.

In the early 80s, his marriage fell apart after he came out as gay. He was diagnosed with HIV in 1988. At the time, there was only one drug approved to treat the disease, and a diagnosis often meant a death sentence.

With StoryCorps, Harris remembered how he came to work with the Atlanta Buyers Club, which distributed medications from the black market to people with HIV before the drugs had been approved by the FDA.

David and Carolyn are volunteers at St. Joseph Hospital in Orange, California, where they sit at the bedside of dying patients. David has been doing these vigils since 2008; Carolyn began in 2011.

column5: A mortician and his wife reminisce about the early days of their romance | StoryCorps
column6:
Many StoryCorps conversations touch on love, work, and death. But when Lynne Houston and her husband, Greg, sat down for their interview, they covered all of that and more just by talking about their first date.

They met 25 years ago in Buffalo, New York. Lynne worked at a restaurant across the street from the funeral home where Greg was a mortician.

Greg charmed Lynne, despite his work bleeding into their romance. When Greg picked her up for dates, he would sometimes be accompanied by an occasional corpse from the hospital. After six months, the couple took a romantic weekend away and drove through upstate New York — in his hearse.

Lynne and Greg eventually married on All Souls Day and now live in McLeansville, North Carolina, where they recorded with StoryCorps.

column5: Ronald Clark remembers living inside a branch of the New York Public Library | StoryCorps
column6:
During the 1940s, custodians who worked for the New York Public Library often lived inside the buildings they tended. In exchange for cleaning and keeping the building secure at night, the library provided an apartment for the custodian and their families.

Ronald Clark’s father, Raymond, was one of those custodians. For three decades he lived with his family on the top floor of the Washington Heights branch on St. Nicholas Avenue in upper Manhattan. Three generations of the Clark family resided in that library until Ronald’s father retired in the late 1970s.

column5: Former neo-Nazi skinhead talks to the man who helped turn his life around | StoryCorps
column6:
In the 1990s, Johnny Holmes was head of security at a high school in Blue Island, Illinois, located just outside of Chicago, where he met Christian Picciolini, a teenage student who was the leader of a local neo-Nazi group.

Christian was involved for eight years before he renounced the movement’s racist principles. Today, he devotes himself to helping others leave hate groups.

He credits Johnny with being the person who helped turn him around; they came to StoryCorps to remember how it happened.

Christian founded EXIT Solutions, a global organization of former extremists with a mission to help people to leave hateful and violent ideologies.

Johnny now serves on his local school board.

column6:
Air travel can be a stressful experience for just about anyone. But for 26-year-old Russell Lehmann, a flight delay or cancellation isn’t just a small inconvenience. He was diagnosed with autism at age 12, and unexpected changes can cause him to have a meltdown — when sensory overload causes him to lose control and break down crying.

That’s what happened when he tried to catch a flight from Reno, Nevada to Cincinnati. At StoryCorps, Russell sat down with David Apkarian, an airline employee, to remember that difficult day.

column6:
In the aftermath of the 2016 presidential race, many families are finding their viewpoints incompatible with those of even their closest relatives. So rather than spend their time constantly arguing, they have agreed to just avoid discussing politics all together.

Jenn was younger, she considered Peter to be her best friend. She played softball—which she hated—because Peter liked baseball; he coached her team because he thought she wanted to play. But as she got older and left for college, their views grew further apart, making it difficult for them to talk about many of the things that are most important to each of them.

Jenn and Peter Stanley came to StoryCorps to try to put their differences aside, and listen to each other’s points of view.

column5: Two nurse practitioners talk about treating  infants exposed to opioids | StoryCorps
column6:
Kyle Cook and Carla Saunders are neonatal nurse practitioners at East Tennessee Children’s Hospital in Knoxville.

They’ve spent decades caring for infants, but when the opioid crisis began to hit in 2010, their jobs changed in ways they never anticipated.

Tennessee has seen a sharp increase in babies born with Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS), a condition marked by tremors and constant shaking in babies who experience withdrawal. In fact, over the past decade, the incidence of babies born with NAS in the state has risen nearly ten-fold.

Kyle and Carla came to StoryCorps to remember when they began to notice how this affected their patients firsthand.

column5: This pilot is headed to space with or without NASA | StoryCorps
column6:
When Wally Funk was 8 years old, she jumped off the roof of her barn while wearing a Superman cape, hoping to fly. That desire never left her, and as an adult, she became a pilot and flight instructor. But for Wally, the ultimate destination was always outer space.

She almost got the chance to go in 1961. That year, she was part of a group of female pilots who took part in tests to determine if women were fit for space travel. The project was run by the same doctor who developed tests for NASA astronauts.

The women, who became known as the Mercury 13, passed many of the same tests as the men but never got to go to space. More than half a century later, Wally Funk hasn’t given up.

She was interviewed in Dallas by one of her flight students, Mary Holsenbeck.

Wally bought a ticket for Richard Branson’s Virgin Galactic and hopes to be on board its maiden voyage into space.

column5: An American solider and Iraqi interpreter talk about becoming close friends | #WhoWeAre
column6:
"My American soldier became my Iraqi brother." -Philip Morris

In 2009, Sergeant Paul Braun was serving near Basra, Iraq with the 34th Military Police Company of the Minnesota Army National Guard. His company was assigned an interpreter, who they nicknamed Philip.

Paul and Philip grew close during Paul’s deployment, and upon returning to the U.S., Paul sponsored Philip’s visa. In 2013, Philip emigrated to the U.S., moving in with Paul in his home in Minnesota, but he had to leave wife and children behind.

In October 2014, Philip and Paul sat down to talk about their friendship and fears for Philip’s future just three weeks before Philip returned to Iraq to try to bring his family back to the U.S.

Two years later—on October 13, 2016—Philip’s wife and children arrived safely in the U.S., reuniting with Philip and joining Paul and his family in their new home in Minnesota.

"Winnie the Pooh" 
by A. A. Milne
Illustrations by Ernest H. Shepard
Originally Published by 
Methuen Publishing in London, 1926.


Chapter 2. Pooh Goes Visiting and Gets Into a Tight Place 
READ ALOUD


Created by A A Milne in 1924, Winnie the Pooh first appeared in a collection of stories in the London Evening News and later in his own titular book in 1926. He was based on the toy bear by the same name, bought for his son, Christopher Robin. Yes, THAT Christopher Robin, along with Christopher's other stuffed animals, Piglet, Kanga, Roo, Tigger and Eeyore. Owl and Rabbit were later created for the book, and Gopher who appears in the Disney anthology movie, "The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh," (1977) was made for the movie - hence his line and play on words, "I'm not in the book!"

'Before writing Winnie-the-Pooh, A. A. Milne was already a successful writer who wrote for the British humor magazine "Punch", had published a mystery novel and was a playwright. Milne began writing poetry for children and later compiled his first verses for publishing, and though his publishers were initially hesitant to publish children's poetry, the poetry collection When We Were Very Young (1924) was a success. It was through this project he met and first collaborated with illustrator E H Shepard.

Among the characters in When We Were Very Young was a teddy bear that Milne modelled after one belonging to his son, Christopher Robin. With the book's success, Shepard encouraged Milne to write stories about Milne's young son  and his stuffed toys, especially the bear he called "Winnie-the-Pooh". Christopher got the name "Winnie" from a bear at the London Zoo, Winnipeg. "Pooh" was the name of a swan they nicknamed while at a stay at the children's hospital.

Milne used Christopher and his toys as inspiration for a series of short stories, which were compiled and published as Winnie-the-Pooh. The model for Pooh remained the bear belonging to Shepard's son. The books of course went on to become a huge success and are now more commonly associated with the Disney franchise.  Penguin Books has called When We Were Very Young, Winnie-the-Pooh, Now We Are Six, and The House At Pooh Corner "the basis of the entire Pooh canon."

On a side note, Winnie the Pooh was HUGE in the late 70's and was everywhere you looked in a Sears & Roebuck, which to translate those last few words to the younger generation, if Amazon was an indoor theme park. But to go on, Winnie the Pooh was huge in my childhood and I had a little doll that had a music box inside that when you wound it, it played the Winnie the Pooh theme. I slept with that doll just about every night until I was six and replaced it with  Gizmo from Gremlins. Signs of the times. All the same, that little yellow bear meant a lot. 

It was a marker of my childhood, and a memory that reminded me, 'whatever happens to us on the way, in that enchanted place on the top of the Forest, a little child and their Bear will always be playing.'

For more Winnie the Pooh
check out "When We Were Very Young", "Now We Are Six", and "The House At Pooh Corner" by A. A. Milne

by Todd Boss

Inspired by the beautiful true story of a nonverbal boy moved to speech at his first Mozart concert, this picture book is a testament to the power of art and the boundless joy it can bring.

When Grandfather comes to take his grandson to a concert, Ronan is quiet as they leave the house, quiet in the car, and quiet at the concert hall. But when the performance is over and the beautiful music fades out at last, Ronan opens his mouth…and lets out a great big WOW!

Not any old WOW, but Ronan’s very first WOW! That one word fills up the hearts of Ronan’s family, the musicians, the audience, and—when the recording goes viral—the world. A beautiful story for ALL families of ALL ages that can see the true power of music, family, and a child's wonder.
